title: Game Over

jokes.text: Carol, they're towing your car! / Damn it. My kids are in there.
jokes.setup: A fertility doctor is giving a heartfelt speech about her personal struggle to conceive, creating an intimate medical moment.
jokes.punchline: The scene is interrupted by a car being towed with her children still inside — a completely absurd non-sequitur that treats child endangerment as a minor inconvenience.
jokes.explanation: Effective cold open misdirection — the sincere emotional setup is violently undercut by chaos. The 'My kids are in there' line lands because it's treated with the same casual energy as a parking ticket. Good economy; wastes no words.

jokes.text: This is Westchester? I am lost.
jokes.setup: A patient came all the way to Westchester to avoid running into someone — implying a deliberate, effortful journey.
jokes.punchline: She reveals she didn't even know she was in Westchester, having gotten there by accident, making the entire premise of avoiding someone collapse.
jokes.explanation: Four words that completely reframe the prior setup. The economy is excellent — maximum comedic information with minimum words. Fits Liz's hapless, self-sabotaging character perfectly.

jokes.text: That's a euphemism, right? / No, my husband and I are trying to conceive. / I'm gonna write you a prescription for progesterone injections. That's a female hormone. Now, I know what you're thinking, and the answer is no. If a man takes it, he won't grow breasts, although that would be awesome.
jokes.setup: Dr. Spaceman gives a standard medical explanation about progesterone injections.
jokes.punchline: He pre-emptively addresses whether men would grow breasts — and expresses genuine disappointment that they won't, wishing they would.
jokes.explanation: This is peak Dr. Spaceman: the 'although that would be awesome' is a beautiful character-specific button. Only Spaceman would mourn the impossibility of iatrogenic male breast growth. The pre-emptive address to 'what you're thinking' is a classic misdirection structure — we expect reassurance, get longing instead. High character integration score is justified.

jokes.text: No money for the whorehouse? That's fine. I'll just look down while hiding my crotch with an oriental fan.
jokes.setup: A non-sequitur aside from Dr. Spaceman with no clear connection to the medical consultation happening.
jokes.punchline: He narrates a completely unrelated internal fantasy/scenario involving a whorehouse and modesty props — as if thinking out loud mid-appointment.
jokes.explanation: Pure Spaceman absurdism. It has no setup in the traditional sense — the joke is the total disconnect between the medical context and his muttered aside. The specificity of 'oriental fan' elevates it from random to vividly absurd. Structurally it's a non-sequitur so structure score suffers, but character integration is high.

jokes.text: Are you Dr. Leo Spaceman? / Come with us to Washington. You've just been named surgeon general of the United States. / Hey, that's a series wrap on Leo Spaceman, suckers. Bye.
jokes.setup: Men in suits arrive at Dr. Spaceman's office mid-scene.
jokes.punchline: The most visibly incompetent doctor on television is named Surgeon General. Spaceman's fourth-wall-adjacent 'series wrap on Leo Spaceman, suckers' breaks the scene entirely.
jokes.explanation: This is an exceptional comedic moment on multiple levels. The irony of the most dangerous quack doctor being elevated to the nation's top medical position is a sharp institutional satire. Then Spaceman's immediate meta-commentary ('series wrap on Leo Spaceman, suckers') breaks the fourth wall in a way that feels earned — it's both a character moment AND a meta-joke about recurring guest characters. The 'suckers' is the perfect button. One of the episode's strongest jokes.

jokes.text: Liz Lemon, that stuff will shrink your testicles, but there are bad side effects as well.
jokes.setup: Tracy walks in concerned about what Liz might be taking, warning her about drugs and their effects.
jokes.punchline: He warns about testicular shrinkage as the primary concern — followed by 'but there are bad side effects as well,' implying testicle shrinkage is fine but something else is worse.
jokes.explanation: The structure here is nearly perfect. The first clause (testicular shrinkage warning to a woman) is already absurd, but the 'but there are bad side effects as well' is the killer — it implies shrinking testicles you don't have is acceptable, but something worse lurks. The economy is superb. Deeply Tracy-specific in its cheerful obliviousness. This earns its high score.

jokes.text: Now, I'm not a woman, so of course I can say whatever I want.
jokes.setup: Tracy is about to comment on Liz's fertility treatments and prefaces his opinion.
jokes.punchline: He states the logical inverse of what one would expect — framing not being a woman as a license to speak freely rather than a reason to hold back.
jokes.explanation: Sharp observational inversion — the logic is exactly backwards from what social norms would suggest, and Tracy delivers it with perfect confidence. It works as both character comedy and social commentary. Very economical.

jokes.text: This seems really weird and unnatural. 'Side effects include mood swings, increased irritability, and swelling of one or more boobs.'
jokes.setup: Tracy criticizes fertility treatments as weird, then immediately reads from the prescription label.
jokes.punchline: 'Swelling of one or more boobs' — the medical precision of 'one or more' applied to such informal language is absurd. Tracy reading it aloud as evidence of weirdness while himself being demonstrably weird.
jokes.explanation: The comedy lands on 'one or more boobs' — the bureaucratic phrasing applied to body parts is a reliable joke template. Tracy as the voice of medical skepticism is good irony. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I'm about to start shooting my Harriet Tubman movie, and I got Octavia Spencer to play the lead... Harriet something.
jokes.setup: Tracy announces his prestigious historical film starring Octavia Spencer.
jokes.punchline: He trails off and can't remember Harriet Tubman's last name — suggesting he doesn't know the basic facts about the film he's directing.
jokes.explanation: The pause and 'Harriet something' is beautifully timed. It's deeply Tracy — he's passionate about projects he doesn't actually understand. The joke also functions as a subtle cultural irony (Black director making a film about a Black historical icon and not knowing her name). Strong character integration.

jokes.text: You know, I once played Frederick Douglass in a one-woman show that the University of Maryland Diamondback called 'too confusing to be offensive.'
jokes.setup: Tracy mentions his Harriet Tubman film, prompting Liz to offer her Civil War-era credentials.
jokes.punchline: The review quote 'too confusing to be offensive' is a devastating and specific form of critical dismissal — suggesting the show failed even at being provocative.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Too confusing to be offensive' is extraordinarily original — it inverts the expected critical failure mode (being TOO offensive) to reveal an even worse fate (being too incoherent to even land the offense). The specificity of 'University of Maryland Diamondback' (a student newspaper) adds to the pathetic charm. Highly quotable. Earns its high scores.

jokes.text: She wanted to be cremated, and she ended up dying in a fire. Such a considerate woman.
jokes.setup: Jack expresses condolences to Hank about his mother's passing, then mentions his own mother's death.
jokes.punchline: His mother's wish to be cremated was fulfilled by the manner of her death — and Jack reframes this as considerate, not tragic.
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's finest jokes. The structure is nearly perfect: setup (she wanted cremation) → devastating reveal (she died in fire) → reframe (considerate). The deadpan pivot to 'such a considerate woman' is what makes it transcendent — Jack's emotional remove from tragedy is a character hallmark, and 'considerate' perfectly captures his inhuman cost-benefit framing. Extremely quotable. This competes with the best dark comedy the show has produced.

jokes.text: One... birthday boy always sleeps in the largest tiger cage.
jokes.setup: Jack mentions he has 'very strict birthday rules' and begins listing them.
jokes.punchline: The first rule is sleeping in the largest tiger cage — an insane premise delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'largest' tiger cage (implying options) is what elevates this. Jack's birthday rules are a wonderfully specific bit of world-building absurdism. Good economy; the joke is entirely in that one sentence.

jokes.text: Some of the rules may be specific to my time in Vietnam.
jokes.setup: Jack listed 'sleeping in the largest tiger cage' as a birthday rule.
jokes.punchline: He acknowledges this might be Vietnam-specific — implying there are multiple Vietnam-informed birthday rules and that tiger cages in Vietnam were simply the best accommodation.
jokes.explanation: The callback to joke 12 lands harder than the original. 'May be specific to my time in Vietnam' is extraordinary economy — it implies (a) Jack was in Vietnam, (b) tiger cages there were places people stayed by choice, and (c) there are multiple such rules. The understatement of 'may be' does a lot of work. This is a runner that rewards the audience for catching the implication.

jokes.text: Yes, I understand that Hank Jr. is writing a children's book about a giraffe who learns he doesn't have to work hard.
jokes.setup: Hank mentions his kids are 'creative types' and therefore not fit for business.
jokes.punchline: Jack confirms this assessment with the specific detail of the children's book — a giraffe who learns he doesn't have to work hard is the most anti-industrious possible message.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the book's message ('doesn't have to work hard') inverts the classic children's book moral completely. It's a sharp satire of nepotism culture and the wealthy creative class. The giraffe detail is perfectly chosen — giraffes already have everything (long necks), making the lazy moral even more absurd. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Yeah, but when she gets out of college, she'll be 21. That's the same age I was when I started Kabletown, got married, and had my first white child.
jokes.setup: Jack points out Kaylie is only 15 and therefore too young to lead Kabletown.
jokes.punchline: Hank does the math — she'll be 21 in college — and equates 21 with being fully accomplished, punctuated by 'my first white child' as a seemingly normal milestone.
jokes.explanation: 'My first white child' is a great button — it's specific in a way that implies much ('first'), lands as dark comedy about the character's hidden complexity, and is delivered as a perfectly ordinary life milestone. The list structure (started company, got married, first white child) makes it land harder.

jokes.text: I admit I was skeptical when I first saw your fall schedule. 'What? Is this guy trying to tank the company?' But, boy, you proved me wrong. Celebrity Homonym is the number-one show in America.
jokes.setup: Hank praises Jack for his excellent work at NBC.
jokes.punchline: His evidence of success is 'Celebrity Homonym' — a clearly idiotic fake show concept that is inexplicably the number-one show in America.
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock fake show name that satirizes the real decline of network television. 'Celebrity Homonym' perfectly captures the desperate celebrity-format trend. The setup — Hank's initial fear that Jack was trying to tank the company — doubles as meta-commentary on NBC's actual struggles. Sharp institutional satire.

jokes.text: The word is 'racket.' Okay, 'racket,' like a tennis racket. Sorry. It's the other one. Again? You know what, pal? Why don't you come over here and tell me that?
jokes.setup: A cutaway to Celebrity Homonym in progress, showing a contestant attempting to identify the word.
jokes.punchline: The contestant keeps getting the wrong homonym, and the host escalates to threatening physical violence — a game show host who challenges contestants to fights.
jokes.explanation: The cutaway to the actual show pays off the setup beautifully. The game show host threatening violence is an unexpected escalation. The wordplay on 'racket' (tennis vs. criminal enterprise) is light but functional. The callback structure earns extra points.

jokes.text: "Assistant"? / CEO. / She'll be on the board, learning the ropes, and you'll keep her chair warm. It'll work great, just like Conan and Jay.
jokes.setup: Hank proposes that Jack be Kaylie's 'assistant CEO,' framing it as a positive arrangement.
jokes.punchline: He compares it to Conan O'Brien and Jay Leno — whose succession arrangement famously collapsed in spectacular, humiliating fashion for both parties.
jokes.explanation: Extremely meta for an NBC show to reference the Conan/Jay debacle as an example of something that 'worked great.' The irony is maximally sharp — this is the actual show that replaced Conan's show acknowledging the disaster. Hank's cheerful ignorance of the reference's implications is a great character beat. The split dialogue ('Assistant?' / 'CEO.') is also a nice structural piece.

jokes.text: Have you ever updated your Flash player? It is so sad. What happens to version 11.4?
jokes.setup: Liz is shown crying in what appears to be a hormone-induced emotional state.
jokes.punchline: The source of her devastation is a Flash player update notification — a mundanely modern existential crisis that is absurd in its specificity.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely original — grief for a Flash player version is a perfect absurdist-observational hybrid. 'What happens to version 11.4?' is surprisingly poignant and funny simultaneously. The specificity of the version number is key. This also efficiently communicates Liz's hormone-addled state while being actually funny rather than just plot-functional. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: I'm taking hormone shots to have a baby, you son of a bitch! [Crying] A beautiful little baby.
jokes.setup: Jack asks what's wrong with Liz, who is visibly emotional.
jokes.punchline: She goes from aggressive ('you son of a bitch') to weepy and tender ('a beautiful little baby') within the same sentence, showing the hormonal mood swings at work.
jokes.explanation: The rapid tonal whiplash within one breath is well-executed. 'You son of a bitch' as prelude to 'a beautiful little baby' shows the hormone side effects established earlier paying off. Good structure. The 'you son of a bitch' directed at Jack for simply asking a question is perfectly Liz.

jokes.text: [Laughing] Being a woman is the worst.
jokes.setup: Liz is having a hormone-fueled breakdown in front of Jack.
jokes.punchline: Jack's summary of what he's witnessing, delivered with amusement rather than sympathy — a reductive, cheerfully oblivious assessment.
jokes.explanation: Short, punchy, and perfectly Jack. The laughter that precedes it is key — he's entertained, not sympathetic. The economy is very strong. The joke itself is a slightly familiar male-observing-female-emotion beat, but Jack's specific delivery of it keeps it character-specific enough to work.

jokes.text: I've spent my life trying to win my mother's approval, but she never gave it to me, which means I can't ever stop trying, even when faced with an impossible task... It's exactly the kind of challenge my mother's anti-love prepared me for. I'll make you proud of me yet, Colleen!
jokes.setup: Jack explains his psychological motivation for pursuing the CEO position against impossible odds.
jokes.punchline: He sincerely thanks his dead mother's emotional abuse ('anti-love') for making him pathologically driven, then shouts at her ghost.
jokes.explanation: The term 'anti-love' is a brilliant coinage — precise, dark, and funny. The pivot from self-aware psychological analysis to earnestly shouting at his dead mother is perfect Jack. High character integration because this joke only works with the specific history of Jack and Colleen. The whole sequence builds his character while being genuinely funny.

jokes.text: It'll either be my masterpiece, or I will resign in shame. [Crying] Just like poor Nixon. He did good things in China.
jokes.setup: Liz appears to still be in her hormone-emotional state and comments on Jack's plan.
jokes.punchline: She cries for Nixon and then provides a strange partial defense of him ('He did good things in China') as if this mitigates the resignation in shame.
jokes.explanation: The hormone-addled empathy for Nixon is a good extension of the hormone comedy. 'He did good things in China' as a weeping consolation is nicely absurd — it's also technically true and therefore even funnier. The structure works as a continuation of the emotional breakdown jokes.

jokes.text: Octavia, excellent, you're black.
jokes.setup: Tracy greets Octavia Spencer on set of his Harriet Tubman film.
jokes.punchline: He greets her professional presence by confirming her racial identity as if this is the first and most important thing to verify for a role she's already cast in.
jokes.explanation: Masterclass in economy. Three words that establish Tracy's entire approach to the project: performative, checklist-oriented, oblivious. The joke is also meta — it mocks a certain kind of Hollywood diversity-check mentality. Tracy saying it with satisfaction ('excellent') makes it perfectly character-specific. The period delivery is everything.

jokes.text: Mm. I don't think so. I'm gonna walk in from over here. / But the door. / Well, you're just gonna have to rewrite the script and explain how my character can go through walls.
jokes.setup: Tracy tells Octavia her character enters through a door. Octavia refuses and wants to walk in from a different spot — which has no door.
jokes.punchline: Octavia demands the script be rewritten to give her character the ability to walk through walls, rather than simply using the door.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Tracy Jordan inversion — he's on the receiving end of his own impossible demands. The logic escalation from 'I want to enter from here' to 'rewrite physics' mirrors exactly how Tracy operates. The meta dimension (Octavia Spencer acting like Tracy Jordan) elevates it. Good structure and economy.

jokes.text: Also, I want to wear a t-shirt, promote my website. / But slaves didn't wear t-shirts. / That sounds like a Tracy problem, Tracy.
jokes.setup: Octavia continues adding unreasonable demands to her role in a Harriet Tubman biopic.
jokes.punchline: 'That sounds like a Tracy problem, Tracy' — Octavia dismisses the historical accuracy concern by labeling it his responsibility while using Liz Lemon's signature deflection style.
jokes.explanation: The mirroring of Liz's management style back at Tracy through Octavia is a nice structural touch. 'That sounds like a Tracy problem, Tracy' is the kind of line Liz uses — and having it said TO Tracy is a good reversal. The parenthetical addressing him by name twice adds rhythm.

jokes.text: I'm done for the day. I got to go home and feed my eels. They're not electric, but I have a plan.
jokes.setup: Octavia wraps her unprofessional behavior by announcing she's leaving.
jokes.punchline: She mentions non-electric eels with a plan to make them electric — a completely baffling aside that implies dangerous and unexplained intentions.
jokes.explanation: The 'they're not electric, but I have a plan' structure is excellent — it suggests dangerous competence. It's absurdist but also weirdly coherent. The joke lands better on rewatch when you appreciate how fully Octavia Spencer has adopted Tracy Jordan's persona.

jokes.text: Well, Mr. Donaghy, you asked me to pull out all the stops on this, so I went deep undercover, and I applied for a job as a drama teacher at Kaylie's school.
jokes.setup: Jack asked his PI for information on Kaylie and Len reports on his methods.
jokes.punchline: Going 'deep undercover' means getting a drama teacher job — a thoroughly prosaic and legal activity presented as high-level espionage.
jokes.explanation: The gap between 'all the stops / deep undercover' and 'drama teacher job application' is the joke. Functional misdirection. Sets up the Jan Foster character well but isn't exceptional on its own.

jokes.text: Hi, I'm Ms. Foster, but, please, call me Jan. Boy, Jay-Z and Shakespeare have nothing in common. Or do they?
jokes.setup: Len presents himself in his undercover persona as a drama teacher named Jan Foster.
jokes.punchline: The drama class lesson appears to be about whether Jay-Z and Shakespeare have anything in common — a trendy educational framework delivered with complete earnestness.
jokes.explanation: A quick satire of 'hip' educational methods that connect classic literature to pop culture. The 'Or do they?' delivery is a gentle parody of academic posturing. Light but functional.

jokes.text: FYI... Jan Foster is currently in a 'lesbian relationship' with Ms. Siegal from the math department. / Okay, I don't know why you had to be a woman. / Let me worry about that.
jokes.setup: Len is presenting his undercover work. He has apparently assumed a female identity as Jan Foster and then developed a romantic subplot.
jokes.punchline: The PI developed an unsolicited romantic relationship as part of his cover, and when questioned about why he needed to be a woman, refuses to explain — implying this was a personal rather than professional choice.
jokes.explanation: The comedy escalates perfectly: the female identity is unexpected, the lesbian relationship is more unexpected, and 'let me worry about that' implies this is very much personal. The scare quotes around 'lesbian relationship' in the narration add an additional layer. Good economy and structure.

jokes.text: Banks. Pedal faster, fatties. God, I love how much you disgust me.
jokes.setup: Jack finds Devin Banks teaching a spin class.
jokes.punchline: Banks's greeting to his spin class students is a deeply contemptuous 'Pedal faster, fatties. God, I love how much you disgust me' — he's using his clients' insecurity as a power source.
jokes.explanation: The line is memorable for its naked contempt delivered with affection. 'I love how much you disgust me' is a brilliantly constructed contradiction — it's both insulting and oddly loving, revealing Banks's character entirely in one sentence. The economy is very strong. This is Devin Banks at his most specific.

jokes.text: Isn't that a bit of a gay cliche? / You're the gay one. / Wanting to be with a woman... How gay is that? / You win sex against a man, that's as straight as it gets.
jokes.setup: Jack challenges Banks on the gay cliche of spin class. Banks turns the accusation back on Jack.
jokes.punchline: Banks's logic that 'wanting to be with a woman' is gay and 'winning sex against a man' is straight is completely inverted logic — delivered as if it's sound reasoning.
jokes.explanation: The inverted sexuality logic is genuinely clever — Banks has constructed an alternate framework where competitive male sexuality defines straightness, leaving heterosexual attraction as somehow less 'straight.' 'You win sex against a man, that's as straight as it gets' is a very quotable line. High originality because the logical structure is novel, not just a gay joke.

jokes.text: But you also know that Jack Donaghy always wins. Or have you forgotten the time we played Battleship? Remember A-8? / You peeked.
jokes.setup: Jack makes a grand claim that he always wins, using a past game as evidence.
jokes.punchline: The past game was Battleship — a children's board game — and Banks's rebuttal is 'You peeked,' implying Jack cheated at Battleship.
jokes.explanation: The deflation of Jack's 'I always win' grandiosity to Battleship cheating is perfect. The specific grid coordinate 'A-8' adds a wonderful verisimilitude. The implication that these two powerful men have a Battleship rivalry is absurdly character-specific. Two words ('You peeked') doing tremendous work.

jokes.text: An assload.
jokes.setup: Jack asks rhetorically how much time they've wasted with their 'sparring and gravel-voiced double entendres.'
jokes.punchline: Banks answers the rhetorical question with total literalness: 'An assload.'
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — one word answer to a rhetorical question. The comedy is in the gap between Jack's grandiose framing and Banks's blunt quantification. The economy score is near-perfect. The joke is simple but well-executed.

jokes.text: If we joined forces, we could become the greatest business power duo since Gregory Linens teamed up with Thomas N'Things.
jokes.setup: Jack proposes an alliance with Banks and promises they'd be a great team.
jokes.punchline: His comparison is to 'Gregory Linens' and 'Thomas N'Things' — fake versions of Bed Bath & Beyond's real parent companies, playing on the actual store names (Bed, Bath & Beyond / Linens 'n Things).
jokes.explanation: The wordplay requires recognition of real store names to land, which makes it a slightly insider joke but rewards attentive viewers. 'Gregory Linens' and 'Thomas N'Things' are delightfully specific fake names that sound like real businessmen. The setup as 'greatest power duo' adds to the absurdism of comparing yourself to home goods retailers.

jokes.text: I know certain things, Jack, about Kaylie's father... Certain super-gay things.
jokes.setup: Banks reveals he has leverage — secret information about Kaylie's father.
jokes.punchline: The dramatic build is punctured by 'certain super-gay things' — a deliberately informal, almost teenage descriptor for supposedly serious blackmail material.
jokes.explanation: The tonal drop from noir-ish intrigue to 'super-gay' is a nice deflation. The joke lives in the word 'super-gay' — deliberately casual and slightly juvenile coming from an ostensibly sophisticated character. Economical.

jokes.text: How gay, Banks, on a scale from bear hunting to hunting bears?
jokes.setup: Jack asks Banks to quantify how gay Kaylie's father is.
jokes.punchline: His scale runs from 'bear hunting' to 'hunting bears' — two activities that sound identical but presumably occupy different positions on the cultural gay/straight spectrum (bear hunting as coded straight, hunting bears as coded gay).
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest lines. The scale from 'bear hunting' to 'hunting bears' is a brilliant wordplay construction — the two endpoints sound identical yet somehow encode an entire spectrum of masculine identity. It requires the audience to decode the gay culture reference to 'bears' while also appreciating the absurdity of the almost-identical phrasing. The delivery from Jack — deadpan, sincere — makes it work. Highly quotable and extremely original. Earns the high score.

jokes.text: Very handsome, horrible personality... I'm totally in love with him.
jokes.setup: Banks describes Frederick Poole's grandson Trevor as Kaylie's suspected real father.
jokes.punchline: He ends his character assassination ('horrible personality') with a sincere declaration of love, making the negative assessment irrelevant to his feelings.
jokes.explanation: The list structure (positive, negative, sincere confession) is well-executed. Banks revealing his romantic obsession mid-exposition is good character work. The 'I'm totally in love with him' has an almost teenage honesty that contrasts nicely with the corporate intrigue framing.

jokes.text: Oh, yes. Congratulations. You've moved from the 'well-meaning lesbian' pile to 'found a man, comma, living a lie.'
jokes.setup: Liz calls the adoption agency to update her marital status from single to married.
jokes.punchline: The agency's categories for female applicants include 'well-meaning lesbian' and 'found a man, comma, living a lie' — deeply judgmental internal classifications presented with bureaucratic neutrality.
jokes.explanation: The pile categorizations are excellent comedy writing — 'well-meaning lesbian' and 'found a man, comma, living a lie' are both specific and devastating. The 'comma, living a lie' is the key move — using punctuation to add a qualifier that transforms a positive development into a damning assessment. Highly original, highly quotable. The bureaucratic delivery amplifies the comedy.

jokes.text: So I'll be 46 by the time I get a baby? / Unless you'd like to adopt an older child. I can give you a six-year-old yesterday. Pick a color.
jokes.setup: Liz learns she'll have to wait four years for a newborn adoption.
jokes.punchline: 'I can give you a six-year-old yesterday. Pick a color.' — The agent's breezy 'pick a color' while describing a child is darkly hilarious in its casualness about race selection as if choosing paint swatches.
jokes.explanation: 'Pick a color' is very strong dark comedy — the transactional attitude toward children combined with the paint-swatch casualness is both funny and uncomfortable. 'I can give you a six-year-old yesterday' also has great economy. The whole exchange treats adoption with a darkly comic bureaucratic indifference that the show handles well.

jokes.text: And I always pictured myself getting double-teamed by two The Rocks. But sometimes we have to make compromises.
jokes.setup: Liz says she always pictured herself getting a newborn. Bev pivots to relate.
jokes.punchline: Bev's equivalent unfulfilled dream is being 'double-teamed by two The Rocks' — presented as a parallel personal sacrifice equivalent to not getting a newborn.
jokes.explanation: The structure is great — Bev's version of 'what I always pictured' is shockingly explicit and absurdly specific ('two The Rocks'). The parallel structure makes the comparison between infertility grief and sexual fantasy feel perfectly inappropriate. The deadpan 'But sometimes we have to make compromises' is the perfect button. 'Two The Rocks' specifically (not just 'The Rock') is the detail that makes it.

jokes.text: Jack, how old is too old for a woman to have a baby? / 19.
jokes.setup: Liz asks Jack a sincere question about age and fertility, expecting a thoughtful response.
jokes.punchline: Jack answers instantly: '19.' No elaboration. Total confidence.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. One word answer to a sincere medical question. The specificity of '19' (not 20, not 18) and the total lack of explanation are what make it. The joke requires zero setup beyond the question, and it characterizes Jack completely — his casual antiquated misogyny delivered with total certainty. This is the kind of single-word punchline that the best sitcom writers live for.

jokes.text: Even if they work, at my age, the kid might just come out a ball of fingers. / Steve Forbes was born a ball of fingers. He had the best surgeons money can buy, but you can still tell.
jokes.setup: Liz worries that age-related fertility issues might affect the health of a child.
jokes.punchline: Jack responds by citing Steve Forbes as a real-world example of someone born 'a ball of fingers' who was surgically repaired but still shows signs of it.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional absurdism — 'ball of fingers' is a vivid, horrible image for a birth defect, and citing Steve Forbes as a documented example gives it a fake-real weight. 'You can still tell' is the perfect button — delivered with sincerity, it implies Jack has looked carefully at Steve Forbes and drawn this conclusion. Highly quotable and deeply original.

jokes.text: For every orphan Annie, there's a 30-year-old Russian dwarf who's just pretending to be a child, according to a movie that I watched part of.
jokes.setup: Jack asks if adopting an older child wouldn't be easier. Liz explains her fear of older adoptees.
jokes.punchline: Her nightmare scenario is a 30-year-old Russian dwarf pretending to be a child — sourced from 'a movie I watched part of,' undermining her own research.
jokes.explanation: The '30-year-old Russian dwarf' specificity is absurd but funny. The kicker — 'according to a movie that I watched part of' — is what makes it exceptional. It simultaneously validates Liz's anxiety as character-consistent (she's done this kind of partial research before) and undercuts her credibility completely. The 'part of' is the key word. One of the episode's most quotable moments.

jokes.text: The reason being a week-long party in Stephen Sondheim's sex dungeon. The workmanship down there is exquisite, but it took forever. / Oh, renovations in New York.
jokes.setup: Banks explains how he has evidence about Kaylie's parentage.
jokes.punchline: The evidence comes from a week-long party in Stephen Sondheim's sex dungeon, the quality of which Liz acknowledges with a mundane 'oh, renovations in New York.'
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke that works exceptionally well. 'Stephen Sondheim's sex dungeon' is a wonderful non-sequitur celebrity association, and 'the workmanship down there is exquisite' treats it as a contractor's review. Liz's response — pivoting to mundane New York renovation complaints — is perfectly character-specific and funny in its total acceptance of the premise. The understatement of 'oh, renovations in New York' is a great button.

jokes.text: Teenage girls can't stop looking at their phones. It's like me with paintings of cannons.
jokes.setup: Jack explains how they can get Kaylie's DNA via her phone — she's always on it.
jokes.punchline: He compares teenage phone addiction to his own compulsion to look at paintings of cannons — a deeply specific and absurd personal detail.
jokes.explanation: The cannon paintings detail is a masterclass in character-specific comedy. It adds nothing to the plot — it exists purely as characterization — and it's funnier for that reason. 'Paintings of cannons' specifically (not photos, not actual cannons) is the key detail. Only Jack Donaghy could be addicted to this specific thing. High character integration justified.

jokes.text: We need a teenage girl. Or someone who thinks like one. / Damn it. Why do I keep helping you? I'll just do anything for approval. I would have been a Nazi.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz discuss needing a teenage girl to get close to Kaylie. Jack looks at Liz.
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately understands she's the candidate, and her self-lacerating explanation ('I would have been a Nazi') is both funny and revealing about her need for approval.
jokes.explanation: 'I would have been a Nazi' is a bold, dark character confession delivered with complete sincerity. It's funny because it's a massive escalation from 'I like approval' to historical atrocity, but also because it contains a kernel of Liz's actual character — her desperate need for validation drives most of her bad choices. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: Let's destroy her.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz have just realized they need someone immature and vicious enough to get close to Kaylie. Cut to Jenna.
jokes.punchline: Jenna appears already committed — 'Let's destroy her' — before anyone has even explained the situation to her. She's enthusiastically pre-agreed to destruction.
jokes.explanation: The comedic structure is nearly perfect: build to 'who do we know who's immature and vicious enough' → cut → Jenna already mid-evil. The cut itself is the joke. 'Let's destroy her' as an opener, without context, before briefing — it's pure Jenna. The economy is maximal. One of the best-structured cuts in the episode.

jokes.text: So how's the movie going? / Terrible. Octavia won't do anything I tell her to do. She left early. She's completely unprofessional. / I don't know, Tray. Sound like she acting like you. / But I'm impossible to deal with. No one has ever been able to rein in my hilarious antics.
jokes.setup: Tracy complains about Octavia Spencer's behavior on set.
jokes.punchline: Tracy, oblivious to the irony that he's describing himself, insists 'I'm impossible to deal with' as if this is a unique distinction — while the implication is that this is exactly Liz Lemon's daily experience.
jokes.explanation: The joke is structural irony — Tracy complaining about someone being Tracy Jordan, while being proud of being the impossible original. 'Hilarious antics' as self-description is wonderfully self-unaware. Good character integration; this is a show-length joke about Tracy's obliviousness finally made explicit.

jokes.text: Jack, pleasure's the name of a pony I hate.
jokes.setup: Jack greets Kaylie with 'to what do I owe the pleasure?'
jokes.punchline: Kaylie rejects the pleasantry entirely by defining 'pleasure' as a pony she hates — completely deflating the formal greeting.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The structure is flawless: formal greeting → unexpected redefinition → hostile specificity. 'A pony I hate' is the exact right detail — ponies are associated with childhood joy, and hating yours is a perfect piece of Kaylie's character. The joke also establishes Kaylie as Jack's equal in quick wit. Extremely quotable. Earns its high scores with a beautiful economy.

jokes.text: Oh, her brain's like silly putty, a toy I am too old for.
jokes.setup: Jack asks what Kaylie did to Jenna.
jokes.punchline: Kaylie compares Jenna's brain to Silly Putty — impressionable and shapeable — then catches herself and adds 'a toy I am too old for,' acknowledging her own youth while being conspicuously mature.
jokes.explanation: The Silly Putty metaphor is sharp and original. The self-correction — 'a toy I am too old for' — adds a perfect layer of character comedy. It's a teenager demonstrating adult-level strategic thinking while also reminding you she's a teenager. The appositive structure ('silly putty, a toy I am too old for') is elegant. Very strong Kaylie characterization.

jokes.text: O.M.G. It's Jenna. You're wearing that belt as a joke, right? / Of course I am. [Laughing] / Where did you get your belt? You're so cool. / Jack is trying to destroy you and wants me to steal your phone.
jokes.setup: Jenna is deployed to befriend Kaylie, first insulting her belt, then immediately complimenting it.
jokes.punchline: After getting Kaylie to drop her guard, Jenna immediately and completely blows the mission by just telling Kaylie exactly what's happening.
jokes.explanation: The structure is perfect comedy writing — quick gain of trust, immediate total betrayal. Jenna immediately telling Kaylie the plan is both character-consistent (Jenna is unreliable and self-interested) and a great structural subversion. The belt joke within the joke also works — the rapid compliment reversal mimics teenage social dynamics perfectly. High character integration; only Jenna would do this.

jokes.text: Kaylie, you look so gorgeous today. I'm wearing a headband because you are.
jokes.setup: After blowing the mission, Jenna tries to recover by pivoting to extreme flattery.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm wearing a headband because you are' — an instant, slavish adoption of a teenager's fashion choice, delivered as if this is a compliment.
jokes.explanation: The immediate headband adoption — presumably she's just put one on — is pathetically good. The cringe is in Jenna's oblivious recovery attempt. 'I'm wearing a headband because you are' is delivered with complete sincerity. Good economy.

jokes.text: Please, I don't keep anything on my phone anymore. I use Gadzorp. / What on Earth is that? / You're so old and out of touch, Donaghy. I might as well be looking at Justin Timberlake.
jokes.setup: Jack's plan to steal Kaylie's phone for DNA fails because she uses 'Gadzorp' — a completely made-up platform Jack doesn't recognize.
jokes.punchline: Kaylie dismisses Jack as technologically ancient by comparing him to Justin Timberlake — a dated celebrity reference that implies Jack is old enough that even culturally relevant figures seem anachronistic next to her.
jokes.explanation: 'Gadzorp' as a fictional teen platform is a good fake word. The Justin Timberlake comparison as an example of 'out of touch' is nice — he's not actually old but to a 15-year-old, presumably. Kaylie's absolute command of the situation is well-established.

jokes.text: I quit, cows. Tell your husbands I tried.
jokes.setup: Jenna appears to be leaving some situation — possibly the spin class or a meeting — and addresses a group of women.
jokes.punchline: She quits and her parting message is 'Tell your husbands I tried' — a bizarrely specific and suggestive farewell that implies some relationship with the women's husbands.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best one-liners. 'I quit, cows' is already strong, but 'Tell your husbands I tried' is exceptional — it implies a whole world of Jenna behavior toward these women's spouses, delivered as a completely normal parting instruction. The line has tremendous quotability and works out of context. Perfect economy. Pure Jenna.

jokes.text: How'd you get these DNA results back so fast? / I happen to have some very powerful friends at the Maury Povich show.
jokes.setup: Jack is surprised by the speed of the DNA results.
jokes.punchline: Banks's powerful connections are to the Maury Povich show — famous for paternity tests — treating a trash TV program as a high-level intelligence asset.
jokes.explanation: The gap between 'very powerful friends' and 'Maury Povich show' is the joke — a prestige mismatch that's perfectly pitched. DNA paternity tests being Maury's domain makes the connection feel simultaneously absurd and logical. Good economy.

jokes.text: Look how far we've come, Jack. From enemies to partners to who knows. Come on, let's get a couple of wines in you and just start wrestling.
jokes.setup: Banks celebrates their apparent victory over Kaylie and reflects on their relationship evolution.
jokes.punchline: 'Let's get a couple of wines in you and just start wrestling' — Banks proposes a romantic/sexual activity with Jack using the most casual possible framing, as if wine-and-wrestling is a standard social activity.
jokes.explanation: Banks's unresolved sexual tension with Jack is a running element of their rivalry. 'Just start wrestling' as a euphemism delivered with full seriousness is good. The 'who knows' escalation before it sets up the proposal well.

jokes.text: Blargh. I'm Liz Lemon. I'm in charge! Nerds! I want to have a baby. My boyfriend is a pilot or something. Sandwiches.
jokes.setup: Tracy has decided to manage Octavia by adopting Liz's management style (WWRLXD). He performs his impression of Liz Lemon.
jokes.punchline: His Liz impression consists entirely of: asserting authority, calling people nerds, expressing baby desire, vaguely referencing her husband's job, and 'sandwiches' — a devastating reduction of Liz Lemon to her essential traits.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. Tracy's Liz impression is both wrong and completely right — it hits every real element of her character (control, baby obsession, food, her husband's job she barely tracks) while being absurdly reductive. 'Sandwiches' as the final word is the perfect button — Liz's food obsession reduced to one word. The 'blargh' opener is character-specific nonsense that lands perfectly. High character integration because this joke only works if you know both Tracy and Liz deeply.

jokes.text: I'm a Jedi.
jokes.setup: Octavia challenges Tracy with some form of escalation. Tracy claims to be a Jedi.
jokes.punchline: With complete sincerity and no elaboration, Tracy declares Jedi status — presumably as a competing claim to authority or specialness.
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum economy. Without more context from the scene, the joke is Tracy asserting a completely irrelevant authority. It's a reliable Tracy beat — absurd self-definition — but less sophisticated than some of his other moments in this episode.

jokes.text: I'm not coming to work tomorrow.
jokes.setup: Tracy continues his Liz impression / Octavia stand-off, apparently escalating his method acting.
jokes.punchline: He announces he's not coming to work tomorrow — either as Liz (who frequently threatens this) or as himself playing hardball with Octavia.
jokes.explanation: This joke depends on the visual/performance context more than the words. As a line alone, it's a standard Tracy absurdism. Gets the job done as part of the Tracy/Octavia competition sequence but doesn't stand out.

jokes.text: Actually, Jack, I've decided to continue living as Jan Foster. It's just in all these years as a P.I., I think my greatest disguise was Len Wazniak.
jokes.setup: Len is supposed to report back to Jack after his undercover mission.
jokes.punchline: Len announces he's keeping the female identity 'Jan Foster' — and that 'Len Wazniak' was his greatest disguise, implying Jan Foster is his true self.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Len's entire male identity was the disguise is a beautiful escalation of the running gag. 'My greatest disguise was Len Wazniak' is a genuinely clever line — it inverts the expected P.I. narrative and delivers a character arc in one sentence. The setup from earlier (the lesbian relationship, the 'let me worry about that') all pays off here.

jokes.text: Kaylie, how do I not seen you to join us? / I know what's past your bad time.
jokes.setup: Jack thinks he's won and greets Kaylie with confident sarcasm.
jokes.punchline: Kaylie's response ('I know what's past your bad time') suggests she knows exactly how this will play out — she's been several steps ahead the whole time.
jokes.explanation: This reads as setup for the reversal to come rather than a standalone joke. The lines seem to have minor transcription issues that affect the joke's clarity. Functional dramatic irony but not strong comedy on its own.

jokes.text: Banks, what are you doing? / FYI Kaylie is my best friend, so I sit next to her at the movies. / Why can't she just sit in the middle?
jokes.setup: Banks appears to be switching sides — Jack is confused about the betrayal.
jokes.punchline: Banks explains his loyalty to Kaylie in terms of movie seating — 'I sit next to her at the movies' — a completely mundane expression of friendship that serves as his entire rationale for betrayal. Then Kaylie adds 'why can't she just sit in the middle?' as if this is the actual logistical debate.
jokes.explanation: The movie seating detail as the explanation for corporate betrayal is a nice deflation of the high-stakes drama. Kaylie's 'why can't she just sit in the middle' as a legitimate grievance is funny — treating the seating logistics as the real issue.

jokes.text: Game over, Kaylie. / [Laughs] 'Game over, Kaylie.' [Laughs]
jokes.setup: Jack delivers what he believes is his triumphant moment
jokes.punchline: He then laughs at his own line — twice — suggesting he's been waiting to say 'Game over, Kaylie' and finds it genuinely delightful
jokes.explanation: Jack laughing at his own villain line is a perfect character beat — it reveals his theatrical enjoyment of winning. The repetition (he says it, then laughs, then repeats it) shows he's savoring it, which is funnier than the line itself.

jokes.text: So Jenna is an Ashkenazi Jew with an extra 'Y' chromosome? / What's that, now?
jokes.setup: Jack learns that the DNA sample was from Jenna's glass, not Kaylie's — and reads out the results.
jokes.punchline: The DNA results reveal Jenna is an Ashkenazi Jew with an extra Y chromosome. Jenna's response — 'What's that, now?' — is baffled and slightly concerned.
jokes.explanation: The extra Y chromosome detail is both a science joke (XYY syndrome) and a character joke about Jenna's underlying nature. 'What's that, now?' — Jenna discovering new facts about her own biology mid-plot-twist — is perfect. The combination of Jenna's naïve reaction and the increasingly specific genetic results is very funny. The joke pays off multiple threads simultaneously.

jokes.text: This is why everyone hates you, Jack. We were all talking about it before at the mall.
jokes.setup: Kaylie delivers her triumph speech, explaining why Jack's plotting makes him despised.
jokes.punchline: 'We were all talking about it before at the mall' — the venue for this group consensus about hating Jack is the mall, a quintessentially teenage location, deflating the grandeur of the corporate drama.
jokes.explanation: The mall detail is the perfect specificity to ground Kaylie as a teenager even while she's outmaneuvering a 50-year-old executive. The idea that a corporate conspiracy against Jack Donaghy was organized at the mall is hilarious and perfect. Good economy — the line does both character work and comedy simultaneously.

jokes.text: Yes, I suppose that's one way this could have played out.
jokes.setup: Kaylie has just delivered her entire triumphant reversal speech, apparently convinced she's won.
jokes.punchline: Jack's response implies the entire preceding scene was Kaylie's fantasy of how things could have gone — he's presenting an alternative. The deadpan delivery deflates her entire speech.
jokes.explanation: Structurally brilliant. The line reframes the entire preceding scene as a hypothetical, which means the audience has been watching Kaylie's imagined triumph — and Jack is now calmly offering a different version. The understatement ('one way this could have played out') is perfect Jack — maximum power with minimal words. Excellent structural confidence.

jokes.text: I'll tell him you said that.
jokes.setup: Jack references Len being 'the worst mole ever' as part of his alternate-reality explanation to Kaylie.
jokes.punchline: Len, who is present in the room, responds to being called the worst mole ever with the blandest possible reaction — 'I'll tell him you said that' — as if Len is a different person from himself.
jokes.explanation: Given that Len has just committed to living as Jan Foster, his referring to himself in the third person ('I'll tell him you said that') is a perfect extension of the identity gag. Maximum economy — four words do the work. This is a very efficient callback.

jokes.text: Well, that's impossible. I mailed them myself. / Did you?
jokes.setup: Jack reveals he never sent the DNA results to Hank. Kaylie insists she mailed them herself.
jokes.punchline: Jack's two-word response 'Did you?' is delivered to Kaylie's certainty — the implication being she mailed something, but not what she thought.
jokes.explanation: Two words that completely destabilize Kaylie's position. The economy is perfect — Jack communicates the entire reversal in a question that contains no information. Good structural use of implication. Functions better as a plot beat than pure comedy, but the delivery is where the comedy lives.

jokes.text: A birthday card.
jokes.setup: The entire episode has been a complex corporate espionage plot involving DNA, alliances, and betrayals. Jack says he sent Hank 'something.'
jokes.punchline: His secret weapon — the move that wins the entire game — was a birthday card. The massive misdirection reveals the simplest possible act as the decisive stroke.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best comedic moment. Three words — 'A birthday card.' — pay off the entire plot. The structure is impeccable: 22 minutes of spy games, DNA plots, and corporate warfare, undone by the simplest act of human courtesy. The pause before the reveal, the specificity of what was sent, and Jack's utter calm are all perfect. This is what excellent sitcom writing looks like — the punchline of the entire episode delivered in three words. Earns the highest score.

jokes.text: You sent him something, right, Kaylie? / Kaylie? / I lost. / After college, I'm gonna have to go into publishing and... marry a finance guy and... do charity stuff.
jokes.setup: Kaylie realizes she's lost everything. Jack presses her on what she sent Hank.
jokes.punchline: Kaylie's horror at losing isn't corporate failure — it's the bourgeois fate awaiting her: publishing, finance husband, charity. The devastating banality of the upper-class female trajectory.
jokes.explanation: The escalating dread of 'publishing... finance guy... charity stuff' is delivered with genuine horror — the ellipses suggesting the weight of each fate. This is sharp social satire: losing a corporate power struggle means being consigned to the acceptable upper-class female life. Kaylie's specific devastation makes her more sympathetic and funnier simultaneously. 'Do charity stuff' as the nadir is perfect.

jokes.text: What a loser. You had me mail that birthday card. That didn't need to happen. That was just mean.
jokes.setup: Banks reflects on Jack's victory.
jokes.punchline: Banks's critique isn't of the strategy — he calls it 'mean' for having him mail the birthday card when Jack could have done it himself. Missing entirely that the cruelty was toward Kaylie.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the birthday card functions as a coda. Banks's complaint — about being used as a mailman, not about the broader manipulation — is a nice character beat. 'That was just mean' applied to making someone else mail your card rather than the emotional destruction of a teenager is a good irony.

jokes.text: What's going on here? And where did you get that sweater? Is that from Chico's harvest naturals collection?
jokes.setup: Liz encounters Tracy in her sweater.
jokes.punchline: Her first priority is identifying where he got her sweater — specifically naming it as Chico's 'harvest naturals collection,' a deeply uncool brand, which reveals Liz's fashion choices in one line.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Chico's harvest naturals collection' does a lot of character work quickly. It establishes that Liz shops at Chico's (unflattering) and that Tracy is apparently wearing it convincingly. Good economy of characterization.

jokes.text: Octavia Spencer got arrested for soliciting sex from an undercover police dog.
jokes.setup: Tracy explains why his movie fell apart.
jokes.punchline: Octavia was arrested for soliciting a police DOG — not an undercover officer posing as a dog, but presumably an actual dog serving as an undercover unit.
jokes.explanation: The 'undercover police dog' is a wonderful absurdism — it's unclear if this means a dog working undercover or a cop posing as a dog, and both readings are funny. The utter deadpan delivery as explanation for why a biopic shut down is great. This is the kind of absurdist non-sequitur 30 Rock does better than anyone.

jokes.text: She turned out to be a Tracy Jordan. So, to deal with her, I tried to be a Liz Lemon.
jokes.setup: Tracy explains his management approach to dealing with Octavia.
jokes.punchline: Tracy refers to himself and Liz in the third person as archetypes — 'a Tracy Jordan' and 'a Liz Lemon' — treating them as behavioral categories rather than people.
jokes.explanation: Turning character names into behavioral archetypes is a meta move that works because the show has done enough character work to justify it. 'A Tracy Jordan' and 'a Liz Lemon' feel like real types within the show's universe. The self-awareness without the characters being aware is well-executed.

jokes.text: Hey, those are my glasses. / Oh, and you popped the lenses out? / No, they shattered in a urinal.
jokes.setup: Liz notices Tracy is wearing her glasses as part of his Liz impression — but they're modified.
jokes.punchline: Tracy explains the lenses didn't come out intentionally — they shattered in a urinal, which is both disgusting and raises more questions than it answers.
jokes.explanation: The 'shattered in a urinal' explanation is good Tracy absurdism — it's specific enough to be vivid but raises immediate questions (how? why were glasses in a urinal?) that the show wisely doesn't answer. The exchange has good rhythm.

jokes.text: Like my booger-eating? / Please, let me just have one. I need it, baby.
jokes.setup: Liz is reflecting on Tracy's early bad habits when he joined the show.
jokes.punchline: Tracy interrupts to name his booger-eating as a habit, then reacts to Liz's implied refusal by pleading 'let me just have one. I need it, baby' — suggesting ongoing, unresolved booger dependency.
jokes.explanation: 'I need it, baby' applied to booger-eating is funny because of the addict framing — this is a genuine craving being thwarted by Liz's management. The 'baby' honorific aimed at Liz adds a specific Tracy speech pattern. The absurdism of booger addiction is character-consistent.

jokes.text: Hey, those Lego men were on a rescue mission to save the other Lego men that I swallowed.
jokes.setup: Liz recalls having to stay up all night because Tracy was sick, referencing some incident with Lego men.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's defense: the Lego men he swallowed were being rescued by other Lego men — an entire internal Lego rescue operation happening in his digestive system.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best absurdist moments. The internal logic — the first Lego men needed rescue from Tracy's stomach, so more Lego men were sent in — is perfect. The commitment to the Lego rescue mission narrative is what makes it transcendent. It implies Tracy has a fully developed theory about Lego agency and responsibility. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Hey, remember that thing we talked about the other day, about adopting an older kid? Well, I want to do it.
jokes.setup: The Tracy sequence has been an extended metaphor about Liz's parenting abilities — caring for Tracy like a difficult child.
jokes.punchline: Liz explicitly connects the experience of managing Tracy to her confidence in adopting an older child — the show acknowledges the metaphor and turns it into a plot decision.
jokes.explanation: The callback that closes the adoption plotline works because the show has been careful to make the Tracy-as-difficult-child metaphor run throughout the episode without being too explicit. The moment Liz makes the connection rewards viewers who've been tracking the parallel. Good structure.

jokes.text: Bitch, more than one person works here. / Who is this? / It's Elizabeth Lemon. / Who?
jokes.setup: Liz calls Bev at the adoption agency, having just told her she wants to adopt an older kid.
jokes.punchline: Bev, who opened the episode by recognizing Liz without her last name, now has no idea who 'Elizabeth Lemon' is — a complete reversal of their earlier rapport.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural callback. Bev opens by saying 'I only deal with one person a year, so I know exactly who you are' — now she has no idea who Elizabeth Lemon is. The 'Bitch, more than one person works here' also inverts her earlier self-positioning. 'Who?' as a final word is economically devastating.

jokes.text: Action. / Every dream begins with a... / Line? / Dreamer. / Action. / You have within you... / Line? / Strength and... / I got it. I got it. / Line?
jokes.setup: Tracy attempts to film his movie with Octavia, applying his Liz Lemon management techniques.
jokes.punchline: Octavia doesn't know her lines — at all. The repeated 'Line?' gag suggests she cannot remember a single sentence of the script.
jokes.explanation: The 'Line?' running gag works as an escalating rhythm joke. The repetition is the structure — each 'Line?' confirms Octavia has completely adopted Tracy's unprofessional behavior. The 'I got it. I got it. Line?' is the best beat — the confidence collapse in one moment.

tmdb_overview: Jack asks Devin Banks to help him discredit Kaylie Hooper, Jack's teenage nemesis and KableTown's future CEO. Liz considers her options as she tries to become a mother. Tracy directs Octavia Spencer in his movie.
insight: Season 7's funniest episode: 94.8 score on pure character-absurdist escalation across 76 jokes.
